interactions.label: In heart failure, dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema are symptoms of forward failure

params.question: In heart failure, dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema are symptoms of forward failure caused by reduced cardiac output.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema are symptoms of backward failure, not forward failure. When the left ventricle fails, pressure backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins, forcing fluid into the alveoli. Forward failure (reduced cardiac output) causes fatigue and exercise intolerance.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Dyspnoea and pulmonary oedema arise from backward failure — elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures cause fluid transudation into the alveoli. Forward failure (reduced cardiac output) manifests as fatigue and exercise intolerance instead.

interactions.label: A 65-year-old woman presents with progressive breathlessness and bilateral ankle

params.question: A 65-year-old woman presents with progressive breathlessness and bilateral ankle swelling. Her JVP is elevated to 8 cm above the sternal angle. This finding most directly reflects which of the following?

answers.text: Elevated left atrial pressure due to mitral valve disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Left atrial pressure is reflected in the pulmonary venous circulation, not the jugular veins. The JVP is a measure of right-sided pressures transmitted through the valveless internal jugular vein.

answers.text: Elevated right atrial pressure transmitted to the internal jugular vein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The internal jugular vein has a direct, valveless connection to the right atrium, making the JVP a reliable bedside estimate of right atrial pressure in heart failure.

answers.text: Increased pulmonary artery pressure from primary pulmonary hypertension

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulmonary artery pressure lies upstream of the right ventricle. While pulmonary hypertension can eventually raise the JVP through right heart failure, the JVP itself directly reflects right atrial pressure, not pulmonary artery pressure.

answers.text: Elevated intracranial pressure causing impaired jugular venous drainage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Raised intracranial pressure can impede cerebral venous outflow but does not produce the typical JVP elevation pattern seen in heart failure. The mechanism here is elevated right atrial filling pressure.

overallFeedback.feedback: The JVP reflects right atrial pressure — the internal jugular vein has a valveless connection to the right atrium. This is why the JVP serves as a bedside manometer for right heart filling pressures in heart failure.
Well done. The JVP provides a direct, non-invasive window into right atrial pressure because the internal jugular vein connects to the right atrium without intervening valves.

interactions.label: A 60-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 30%) is haemodynamically stable after initial

params.question: A 60-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 30%) is haemodynamically stable after initial management. According to guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), which prescribing approach is recommended?

answers.text: Start with a diuretic alone and add neurohormonal agents only if symptoms persist

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve mortality. GDMT prioritises the four neurohormonal pillar drugs — diuretics are added as needed for volume management alongside them.

answers.text: Select two of the four pillar drug classes based on the predominant symptom profile

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Current guidelines recommend all four pillar classes, not a selective approach. Each class targets a different component of the neurohormonal cascade, and the mortality benefit comes from the combination.

answers.text: Initiate all four pillar drug classes — ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Every haemodynamically stable HFrEF patient should receive all four pillar classes. Together they reduce all-cause mortality, reduce hospitalisation, and reverse ventricular remodelling.

answers.text: Begin with an ACE inhibitor alone and up-titrate to maximum dose before adding any other agent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sequential single-agent up-titration delays the benefit of the other three pillar classes. Current evidence supports initiating all four pillars with concurrent up-titration as tolerated.

overallFeedback.feedback: GDMT for HFrEF requires all four evidence-based drug classes (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) in every haemodynamically stable patient. Each pillar targets a different neurohormonal mechanism, and together they reduce mortality and reverse remodelling.
Correct. GDMT for HFrEF means all four pillar drug classes for every eligible patient — each targets a different arm of the neurohormonal cascade driving disease progression.

interactions.label: A child with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) has a confirmed left-to-right shu

params.question: A child with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) has a confirmed left-to-right shunt on echocardiography. Which of the following best explains why this child does not have cyanosis?

answers.text: The shunted blood bypasses the pulmonary circulation entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In a left-to-right shunt, oxygenated blood flows from the left heart into the right heart and recirculates through the pulmonary circulation — it does not bypass the lungs.

answers.text: Oxygenated blood crosses from the left to the right heart, so systemic arterial blood remains fully saturated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In a left-to-right shunt, already-oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs. No deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation, so arterial oxygen saturation is maintained and there is no cyanosis.

answers.text: The right ventricle increases its ejection fraction to compensate for the extra volume load

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The right ventricle does adapt to volume overload, but this compensatory response does not explain the absence of cyanosis. Cyanosis depends on whether deoxygenated blood reaches the systemic circulation — and in a left-to-right shunt, it does not.

answers.text: The defect is too small to permit any significant intracardiac blood flow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The echocardiogram has confirmed a left-to-right shunt — significant flow is present. The absence of cyanosis is because the shunt direction keeps deoxygenated blood out of the systemic arterial circulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a left-to-right shunt, oxygenated blood crosses from the left heart to the right heart. Systemic arterial blood remains fully oxygenated because no deoxygenated blood enters the aorta — this is why left-to-right shunts are classified as acyanotic.

Correct. In left-to-right shunts, oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs — systemic arterial blood stays fully saturated, so there is no cyanosis. This is the defining principle of acyanotic congenital heart disease.
